d.desc: Linear Algebra is the mathematics of vectors, matrices, and linear transformations — the most critical math prerequisite for ML.
d.why: Neural networks are chains of matrix multiplications. PCA, SVD, and attention are all linear algebra. Without this you cannot understand what your models compute.

resources.text: Gilbert Strang — Introduction to Linear Algebra (MIT)
numpy.linalg docs — practice every operation in code

d.desc: Calculus gives us the tools to optimize ML models. Derivatives measure how a function changes and gradient descent uses this to minimize loss functions.
d.why: Backpropagation is the chain rule applied to a computation graph. Every optimizer relies on gradients. You cannot debug training without understanding calculus.

resources.text: PyTorch autograd — see calculus in action

d.desc: Descriptive statistics summarizes the main features of a dataset. It is your first lens for understanding data before any model is trained.
d.why: Every ML project starts with EDA. If you cannot describe your data, you will make wrong modelling decisions — garbage in, garbage out.

resources.text: Think Stats by Allen Downey (free PDF)
Kaggle — practice EDA on Titanic, Iris

d.desc: Inferential statistics lets you draw conclusions about a population from a sample. Bayes Theorem is the framework for updating beliefs given new evidence.
d.why: A/B testing, confidence intervals, and Bayesian models all require this. It prevents you from fooling yourself with statistically insignificant results.

d.desc: Python is the dominant language for ML. You need solid fundamentals — clean OOP, data structures, and the ability to write reusable modular code.
d.why: Every ML library is Python. You will write custom layers, data loaders, and pipelines — you need fluent Python, not just hello-world.

resources.text: LeetCode Easy problems — reinforce logic & data structures

d.desc: NumPy provides fast N-dimensional arrays and mathematical operations that form the backbone of every ML library.
d.why: Pandas, scikit-learn, and PyTorch all use NumPy arrays internally. If you cannot vectorize your code your models will be 100x slower.

resources.text: From Python to NumPy by Nicolas Rougier (free PDF)

d.desc: Pandas is the go-to library for data manipulation and analysis. Think Excel in Python — but far more powerful, programmable, and reproducible.
d.why: Real-world data is always messy. You will spend 60-80% of any ML project wrangling data in Pandas.

resources.text: Pandas official docs — 10 minutes to pandas
Python for Data Analysis by Wes McKinney

d.desc: Matplotlib and Seaborn are the core plotting libraries. Visualization is how you understand data, communicate insights, and debug model behaviour.
d.why: A model that cannot be visualized cannot be fully understood or trusted. Charts catch data leakage and class imbalance that tables miss.

resources.text: Kaggle — EDA notebooks on any dataset

Compute mean, variance, std dev manually before using NumPy
Load a CSV with Pandas and print shape, dtypes, null counts
Compute partial derivative of f(x,y) = x²y + 3xy² by hand
Plot a normal distribution and mark mean ± 1σ, 2σ, 3σ with matplotlib

Perform full EDA on Titanic dataset: nulls, distributions, correlations, outliers

Build OOP-based Matrix class with add/mul/transpose/determinant methods
a: Implement gradient descent from scratch using only NumPy, verify on quadratic function
Build a full statistical hypothesis testing module (t-test, chi-square, p-value)
Implement PCA from scratch using eigendecomposition, compare to sklearn PCA

projects.name: 📊 Exploratory Data Analysis Dashboard
projects.desc: Take any real-world dataset (Titanic, House Prices, or COVID data). Clean it entirely with Pandas, perform statistical analysis (mean, median, distributions, outliers, correlation matrix), and produce a complete EDA report with Matplotlib/Seaborn charts. Document every statistical insight with mathematical justification.

meta.v: Linear Algebra, Stats, Pandas, NumPy, Viz

d.desc: ML systems need data from databases, APIs, and IoT streams. Knowing how to acquire structured and unstructured data is the first step in any real pipeline.
concepts: SQL — SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, subqueries
d.why: You will rarely be handed a clean CSV. Production ML systems pull from databases, APIs, and streaming sources.

d.desc: Different data formats serve different performance needs. Knowing when to use CSV vs Parquet vs JSON is a production-level skill.
d.why: Parquet can load 10x faster than CSV for large datasets. Choosing the right format reduces pipeline bottlenecks significantly.

resources.text: Apache Parquet docs — columnar storage explained
Python pickle vs joblib — serialization patterns

d.desc: Real data is almost always dirty — missing values, wrong types, duplicates, inconsistent formatting. Data cleaning is the most time-consuming step in any ML project.
d.why: A dirty dataset produces a broken model. Studies show data scientists spend 60-80% of their time cleaning data.

resources.text: Pandas docs — Working with missing data

d.desc: Feature Engineering transforms raw data into inputs that help models learn better. Feature Selection identifies which features to keep and which to drop.
d.why: The right features can double model accuracy. Feature engineering often matters more than algorithm choice.

resources.text: Feature Engineering for ML by Alice Zheng
Kaggle competitions — study top notebooks for FE tricks

d.desc: Feature Scaling normalizes the range of features so no single feature dominates due to its magnitude. Essential for distance-based and gradient-based models.
concepts: Normalizer — scales each sample to unit norm
Log and power transforms for skewed data
d.why: KNN, SVMs, and neural networks are sensitive to feature scale. Without scaling a feature with range [0,10000] will dominate one with [0,1].

resources.text: Build a StandardScaler from scratch — implement fit/transform
Hands-On ML by Aurelien Geron — Ch. 2

d.desc: High-dimensional data is slow to train on and hard to visualize. Dimensionality Reduction compresses data while preserving the most information.
d.why: Reduces training time, removes noise, enables visualization of high-dim data, and can improve model performance by eliminating redundant features.

b: Connect to SQLite DB, query data, load into Pandas DataFrame
Handle missing values: compare mean imputation vs median vs KNN imputer
Apply MinMaxScaler and StandardScaler, explain why each output differs
Create 3 new features from existing ones on house price dataset

Use SelectKBest and feature importance from Random Forest to compare selection methods

Apply PCA to MNIST: visualize variance explained vs components count

Implement target encoding with cross-validation leak prevention

projects.name: 🔧 End-to-End Data Preprocessing Pipeline
projects.desc: Pull data from a real API (e.g., OpenWeather, Yahoo Finance, or a Kaggle dataset), store it, build a full preprocessing pipeline: clean → engineer features → scale → reduce dimensions → export clean dataset. Use sklearn Pipelines. Document what each step changes about the data with before/after stats.

meta.v: Data Sources, Cleaning, FE, Scaling, PCA

topics.name: Types of ML (Supervised / Unsupervised / RL / Self-Supervised)

d.desc: Understanding the landscape of ML — supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and self-supervised learning — is the conceptual foundation before diving into any specific algorithm.
concepts: Self-Supervised Learning — labels from data itself
Key applications and industry use cases for each type
d.why: Choosing the wrong learning paradigm is a fundamental mistake. Knowing when you have a supervised vs unsupervised problem shapes every downstream decision.

resources.text: Google ML Crash Course — free, well structured
Hands-On ML by Aurelien Geron — Chapter 1

d.desc: Linear Regression finds the best-fit line through data to predict a continuous output. The simplest and most interpretable ML model — and the conceptual seed of deep learning.
d.why: Understanding linear regression deeply gives you the intuition to understand every more complex model that follows.

resources.text: Andrew Ng ML Course — linear regression from scratch
Implement with NumPy only, then verify with sklearn

d.desc: Polynomial Regression adds polynomial features to capture non-linear relationships while keeping the algorithm linear in its parameters.
concepts: Regularization as the cure for high-degree polynomials
d.why: Real-world data is rarely linear. Polynomial regression is the bridge between linear models and neural networks, perfectly illustrating overfitting.

resources.text: Plot train vs test error as degree increases — observe overfitting

d.desc: Logistic Regression predicts the probability of a binary class using the sigmoid function. The foundation for understanding classification in ML.
d.why: Logistic regression is still used in production at scale (e.g., Google ads CTR). Deep learning classification heads are logistic regression.

resources.text: Implement sigmoid, log-loss, gradient descent from scratch

d.desc: Decision Trees split data hierarchically based on feature thresholds. Random Forest combines hundreds of trees with bagging and random feature subsampling.
d.why: Random Forest is one of the most robust ML algorithms — handles mixed data types, missing values, and non-linear relationships without much tuning.

d.desc: SVMs find the optimal hyperplane that maximizes the margin between classes. Kernel functions allow SVMs to handle non-linearly separable data.
concepts: Kernel Trick — RBF, polynomial, sigmoid kernels
d.why: The kernel trick and concept of margin are foundational ideas referenced throughout ML theory. SVMs are still competitive on small-medium tabular datasets.

resources.text: sklearn.svm.SVC — compare linear vs RBF boundaries
libsvm paper — understanding the algorithm deeply

d.desc: KNN classifies a point by majority vote of its k nearest neighbours. No training — pure memorization of the dataset at inference time.
concepts: Curse of dimensionality — why KNN fails in high dims
KD-Tree and Ball-Tree for fast lookup
Weighted KNN — closer neighbours vote more
d.why: KNN illustrates the importance of feature scaling and the right distance metric. It motivates why we need smarter algorithms for large data.

resources.text: Visualize decision boundaries for different k values

d.desc: Gradient Boosting builds an ensemble of trees sequentially, each correcting the errors of the previous. XGBoost and LightGBM dominate structured data competitions.
concepts: XGBoost — regularization, tree pruning, parallel build
d.why: XGBoost and LightGBM win the majority of Kaggle tabular competitions. Top choice for fraud detection, credit scoring, and recommendation ranking.

resources.text: Microsoft LightGBM docs — leaf-wise vs level-wise

d.desc: Clustering groups data points by similarity without labels. K-Means finds spheres, DBSCAN finds arbitrary shapes, GMM gives probabilistic assignments.
d.why: Customer segmentation, anomaly detection, document grouping — all use clustering. First algorithm to reach for with unlabelled data.

resources.text: scikit-learn clustering docs — comparison of algorithms

topics.name: Model Evaluation Metrics (Accuracy, F1, ROC-AUC, Confusion Matrix)

d.desc: Model evaluation metrics measure whether your model is actually good. Accuracy alone is dangerously misleading — especially with class imbalance.
concepts: Confusion Matrix — TP, FP, TN, FN
Log-loss and calibration for probability models
d.why: A model 99% accurate on fraud data might never detect fraud. Using the right metric is the difference between a safe and a dangerous model.

resources.text: Kaggle — evaluation section of each competition

d.desc: Validation techniques give an unbiased estimate of model performance on unseen data. Without proper validation you will overfit to your test set.
concepts: Time-Series CV — no future data leakage
d.why: Data leakage is the #1 reason models fail in production. Proper validation is the only way to get a realistic performance estimate.

resources.text: Implement K-Fold from scratch to understand the mechanics

d.desc: Regularization adds a penalty to the loss function to discourage overly complex models. Ridge (L2), Lasso (L1), and ElasticNet are the three main variants.
concepts: L1 Regularization (Lasso) — sparse weights, feature selection
ElasticNet — hybrid of L1 and L2
Dropout in neural networks — same intuition
d.why: Overfitting is universal in ML. Regularization is the primary defence. Lasso can simultaneously fit a model and select features.

resources.text: Plot coefficient paths as alpha increases — understand sparsity

Train logistic regression on Iris dataset, print confusion matrix
Run K-Means clustering on 2D data, visualize cluster centroids evolving per iteration
Plot ROC-AUC curve for binary classifier, explain what AUC=0.5 means vs AUC=1.0
i: Compare Decision Tree depth vs accuracy/overfitting on train vs test sets with plots
Train XGBoost on tabular dataset, tune n_estimators, max_depth, learning_rate with GridSearchCV

SVM: compare linear vs RBF kernel, explain decision boundary shape differences

Build full model selection framework: train 5 models, K-Fold each, compare by F1-macro, select best
Implement DBSCAN from scratch, compare to K-Means on non-spherical cluster data

projects.desc: Full regression pipeline on Kaggle House Prices dataset. Preprocess → engineer features → compare Linear, Polynomial, Ridge, Lasso, Random Forest, XGBoost. Validate with K-Fold. Report RMSE, R² for each. Select best model with justification.

meta.v: Model comparison report + best model saved

projects.name: 🎯 Customer Segmentation System
projects.desc: Use a retail/e-commerce dataset. Apply K-Means, DBSCAN, Hierarchical clustering. Reduce dims with PCA first. Evaluate clusters with silhouette score. Assign business-meaningful labels to each segment. Build a reusable segmentation module.

d.desc: A neural network is composed of layers of artificial neurons (perceptrons). The MLP is the foundational architecture — understanding it unlocks all of deep learning.
concepts: MLP — input layer, hidden layers, output layer
d.why: Every advanced architecture (CNN, RNN, Transformer) is built from the same building blocks as the MLP. The perceptron is the foundation of the entire deep learning stack.

resources.text: Implement a 2-layer MLP from scratch in NumPy (XOR)
Neural Networks and Deep Learning by Michael Nielsen (free)

d.desc: Forward propagation computes predictions. Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss w.r.t. every weight using the chain rule — enabling gradient descent to train the network.
concepts: Chain Rule applied to nested functions
Gradient of MSE and Cross-Entropy w.r.t. weights
d.why: Backpropagation is the single algorithm that makes deep learning work. Without understanding it you cannot debug training failures or exploding gradients.

resources.text: Implement backprop from scratch in NumPy — do not skip this

d.desc: Activation functions introduce non-linearity so networks can learn complex patterns. Loss functions measure the error between predictions and ground truth.
concepts: Sigmoid, Tanh — saturation and vanishing gradient
Leaky ReLU, ELU, GELU — solving dying ReLU
d.why: Choosing the wrong activation in deep networks causes vanishing gradients. The right loss function defines what your model actually optimizes for.

resources.text: Plot activation functions and their gradients

d.desc: PyTorch, TensorFlow, and Keras provide automatic differentiation, GPU support, and pre-built layers — eliminating the need to implement backprop manually.
concepts: nn.Module — defining custom layers and models
Training loop: forward -> loss -> backward -> step
d.why: PyTorch is the dominant framework for research and production. Knowing it deeply means you can implement any architecture from a paper.

resources.text: Build MNIST classifier with PyTorch from scratch

d.desc: CNNs use convolutional filters to detect spatial hierarchies in images — edges, textures, objects. They are the backbone of computer vision.
d.why: Every production vision system (face recognition, medical imaging, autonomous driving) is built on CNNs. This is the entry point to computer vision.

resources.text: Build CNN for CIFAR-10 in PyTorch from scratch
ResNet paper — Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

d.desc: CNNs power tasks beyond classification — semantic segmentation (pixel labels), object detection (bounding boxes), and video understanding.
concepts: Object Detection — YOLO, Faster R-CNN, SSD
d.why: Knowing CNN applications separates someone who trained MNIST from someone who can build real vision products.

resources.text: YOLO paper series — fast object detection
torchvision — pretrained models and detection datasets
U-Net paper — semantic segmentation for medical imaging

d.desc: RNNs process sequential data by maintaining a hidden state. LSTMs and GRUs solve the vanishing gradient problem enabling learning of long-range dependencies.
concepts: Bidirectional RNN — reads sequence both ways
d.why: Understanding RNNs is required to understand attention mechanisms and Transformers — their natural evolution.

resources.text: Build char-level language model with LSTM in PyTorch

d.desc: Attention mechanisms allow models to focus on relevant parts of an input — solving the bottleneck of encoding entire sequences into a single fixed vector.
concepts: Scaled Dot-Product Attention — Q, K, V matrices
Self-Attention — attending to the same sequence
d.why: Attention is the direct predecessor of Transformers. Understanding the Q/K/V mechanism is required to understand BERT, GPT, and every modern LLM.

resources.text: Attention Is All You Need paper (Vaswani et al., 2017)
Implement scaled dot-product attention from scratch in PyTorch

d.desc: Autoencoders learn a compressed latent representation of data through an encoder-decoder structure trained to reconstruct its input.
concepts: Encoder — compresses input to latent code z
d.why: Autoencoders underpin dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection, image generation (VAE), and are the conceptual precursor to diffusion models.

resources.text: Lilian Weng blog — From Autoencoder to Beta-VAE
Build denoising autoencoder on MNIST in PyTorch
VAE paper — Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes (Kingma & Welling)

d.desc: GANs train two networks in adversarial competition — a generator produces fake data, a discriminator tries to distinguish fake from real. The result: photorealistic generative models.
d.why: GANs produced the first photorealistic synthetic images and remain relevant for data augmentation, style transfer, and image-to-image translation.

resources.text: Original GAN paper — Goodfellow et al. 2014
Build DCGAN for MNIST digit generation in PyTorch
Lilian Weng — From GAN to WGAN (comprehensive blog)

b: Implement a 2-layer MLP from scratch in pure NumPy for XOR problem
Manually compute forward pass and backprop for a 3-neuron network on paper then code it
Build MNIST classifier using PyTorch, achieve >98% accuracy
Compare ReLU vs Sigmoid on same network: plot training loss curves
i: Build CNN from scratch in PyTorch for CIFAR-10, implement conv → pool → FC layers manually
Build an LSTM to predict next character in text sequences (char-level LM)
Implement a denoising autoencoder, visualize original vs encoded vs decoded images
Code scaled dot-product attention from scratch using matrix operations
a: Build a GAN to generate handwritten digits; track generator vs discriminator loss balance
Implement transfer learning: fine-tune ResNet18 on a custom image dataset with only last 2 layers unfrozen

projects.name: 🖼️ Image Classifier with CNN (Transfer Learning)
projects.desc: Build an image classifier for a 5–10 class custom dataset using PyTorch. Train a CNN from scratch first, then apply transfer learning with ResNet/EfficientNet. Compare accuracy, training time, convergence speed. Deploy as a simple inference script.

meta.v: CNN, Backprop, PyTorch, Activation Fns, Transfer Learning
Trained model + inference script + comparison report

projects.name: 📈 Time Series Forecasting with LSTM
projects.desc: Use stock price or weather data. Build LSTM model in PyTorch to forecast next N time steps. Compare vs ARIMA baseline. Tune sequence length, hidden size, layers. Evaluate with MAE, RMSE. Bonus: add attention mechanism on top of LSTM.

d.desc: Transformers replaced RNNs as the dominant sequence model. Using only self-attention (no recurrence), they process sequences in parallel — enabling the LLM revolution.
concepts: Self-Attention — all tokens attend to all tokens
d.why: BERT, GPT, LLaMA, Stable Diffusion — every frontier AI model is a Transformer. This is the single most important architecture in modern AI.

resources.text: Attention Is All You Need paper — read it closely
Implement Transformer encoder from scratch in PyTorch
Jay Alammar — The Illustrated Transformer (essential blog)

d.desc: NLP preprocessing converts raw text into numerical representations. Tokenization, stemming, lemmatization, and word embeddings are the core pipeline steps.
d.why: All NLP starts here. Even with LLMs, understanding tokenization (BPE, SentencePiece) is critical — it affects context length, cost, and multilingual performance.

resources.text: Natural Language Processing with Python (NLTK book, free)
Gensim Word2Vec — train on custom corpus, visualize with t-SNE

d.desc: BERT and GPT are the two dominant pretraining paradigms that power modern NLP — from sentiment analysis to question answering to text generation.
concepts: Sentence classification, NER, QA with BERT
d.why: BERT/GPT-style models are the industry standard for all NLP tasks. If you work with text in production, you will fine-tune or prompt these models daily.

resources.text: HuggingFace — fine-tune BERT for sentiment on IMDB

d.desc: Reinforcement Learning trains agents to take actions to maximize cumulative reward. Q-Learning and DQN use neural networks to approximate optimal action-value functions.
d.why: RL powers game-playing AI (AlphaGo), robotics control, and RLHF — the training technique behind ChatGPT.

resources.text: Sutton & Barto — RL: An Introduction (free PDF)
DQN paper — Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning

d.desc: Policy Gradient methods directly optimize the policy using gradient ascent on expected reward. Actor-Critic combines value-based and policy-based methods.
concepts: Policy function pi(a|s) — parametric action selection
REINFORCE algorithm — Monte Carlo policy gradient
Actor-Critic — separate value and policy networks
d.why: PPO is the algorithm behind ChatGPT's RLHF training and most production robotics. Policy gradient methods handle continuous action spaces that DQN cannot.

resources.text: Spinning Up in Deep RL — OpenAI (free, comprehensive)
PPO paper — Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms

d.desc: Recommendation Systems predict what users will like based on past behaviour and similarities. Collaborative filtering, matrix factorization, and embedding models are the core techniques.
d.why: Recommenders drive revenue at Netflix, YouTube, Amazon, and Spotify. Matrix factorization and embedding models are transferable to any domain.

resources.text: Koren et al. — Matrix Factorization Techniques
Surprise library — collaborative filtering in Python

d.desc: Explainable AI (XAI) provides tools to understand why a model makes specific predictions — critical for trust, debugging, fairness audits, and regulatory compliance.
d.why: In healthcare, finance, and law, black-box models are legally prohibited or ethically unacceptable. XAI is now a production requirement.

resources.text: shap.TreeExplainer — SHAP for XGBoost and Random Forest
Interpretable ML book — Christoph Molnar (free PDF)

d.desc: Self-supervised learning generates supervision from unlabelled data itself. Semi-supervised learning uses both labelled and unlabelled data to improve performance.
concepts: Pseudo-Labelling — confident unlabelled predictions as labels
Label efficiency — how much labelled data is needed?
d.why: Labelling data is expensive. Self-supervised pretraining (BERT, GPT, Vision MAE) achieves strong results with minimal labels. This is how frontier models are trained.

resources.text: SimCLR paper — A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning

projects.desc: Build a dual-task NLP pipeline: sentiment classification (fine-tuned BERT) + topic modeling (LDA). Input: raw text dataset (tweets, reviews). Output: per-document sentiment score + top topics with representative keywords. Add SHAP explanations for sentiment model.

projects.desc: Train a DQN agent to solve a medium-complexity OpenAI Gym environment (LunarLander or CartPole-v1). Implement experience replay, target network, epsilon decay. Log training rewards and plot learning curves. Compare DQN vs random agent baseline.

phases.label: Phase 6: Production
phases.title: Production ML — Deployment, Tuning & Full Systems

d.desc: Model selection picks the best algorithm. Hyperparameter tuning finds the optimal configuration. Together they bridge trained model and production-ready model.
concepts: Randomized Search — random sampling of parameter space
Early Stopping — prevent overfitting during tuning
Warm Starting — continue tuning from previous run
d.why: Default hyperparameters are almost never optimal. Proper tuning routinely improves performance by 5-15%. Bayesian optimization is now the industry standard.

d.desc: Production ML requires robust data pipelines — splitting data correctly, loading batches efficiently, preventing leakage, and handling distributional shift over time.
d.why: More production ML failures are caused by incorrect data pipelines than bad models. A leaky pipeline makes your model look perfect in testing and fail in production.

resources.text: sklearn Pipeline docs — compose preprocessing + model
PyTorch Dataset & DataLoader — custom dataset class

d.desc: Model serving deploys trained models to production. FastAPI + Docker is the standard lightweight stack for ML APIs.
concepts: Model serialization — joblib, pickle, ONNX, TorchScript
FastAPI — async REST API for ML
d.why: A model that is not deployed is worthless. Knowing how to serve models with FastAPI and Docker turns research into product.

resources.text: Build a /predict POST endpoint for an sklearn model

d.desc: Advanced scikit-learn covers building reusable, production-grade pipelines with custom transformers, column transformers, and feature unions.
concepts: ColumnTransformer — different transforms per feature type
FunctionTransformer — wrap any function as transformer
d.why: Clean, reusable sklearn Pipelines prevent data leakage, make deployment trivial, and ensure train/inference consistency. This is how professional ML engineers write production code.

resources.text: Build a custom TextCleaner transformer class from scratch
Hands-On ML by Geron — Pipelines chapter

18.why: Logistic regression is still used in production at scale (e.g., Google ads CTR). Deep learning classification heads are logistic regression.

resources.text: Implement sigmoid, log-loss, gradient descent from scratch

19.desc: Decision Trees split data hierarchically based on feature thresholds. Random Forest combines hundreds of trees with bagging and random feature subsampling.
19.why: Random Forest is one of the most robust ML algorithms — handles mixed data types, missing values, and non-linear relationships without much tuning.

20.desc: SVMs find the optimal hyperplane that maximizes the margin between classes. Kernel functions allow SVMs to handle non-linearly separable data.
concepts: Kernel Trick — RBF, polynomial, sigmoid kernels
20.why: The kernel trick and concept of margin are foundational ideas referenced throughout ML theory. SVMs are still competitive on small-medium tabular datasets.

resources.text: sklearn.svm.SVC — compare linear vs RBF boundaries
libsvm paper — understanding the algorithm deeply

21.desc: KNN classifies a point by majority vote of its k nearest neighbours. No training — pure memorization of the dataset at inference time.
concepts: Curse of dimensionality — why KNN fails in high dims
KD-Tree and Ball-Tree for fast lookup
Weighted KNN — closer neighbours vote more
21.why: KNN illustrates the importance of feature scaling and the right distance metric. It motivates why we need smarter algorithms for large data.

resources.text: Visualize decision boundaries for different k values

22.desc: Gradient Boosting builds an ensemble of trees sequentially, each correcting the errors of the previous. XGBoost and LightGBM dominate structured data competitions.
concepts: XGBoost — regularization, tree pruning, parallel build
22.why: XGBoost and LightGBM win the majority of Kaggle tabular competitions. Top choice for fraud detection, credit scoring, and recommendation ranking.

resources.text: Microsoft LightGBM docs — leaf-wise vs level-wise

23.desc: Clustering groups data points by similarity without labels. K-Means finds spheres, DBSCAN finds arbitrary shapes, GMM gives probabilistic assignments.
23.why: Customer segmentation, anomaly detection, document grouping — all use clustering. First algorithm to reach for with unlabelled data.

resources.text: scikit-learn clustering docs — comparison of algorithms

24.desc: Model evaluation metrics measure whether your model is actually good. Accuracy alone is dangerously misleading — especially with class imbalance.
concepts: Confusion Matrix — TP, FP, TN, FN
Log-loss and calibration for probability models
24.why: A model 99% accurate on fraud data might never detect fraud. Using the right metric is the difference between a safe and a dangerous model.

resources.text: Kaggle — evaluation section of each competition

25.desc: Validation techniques give an unbiased estimate of model performance on unseen data. Without proper validation you will overfit to your test set.
concepts: Time-Series CV — no future data leakage
25.why: Data leakage is the #1 reason models fail in production. Proper validation is the only way to get a realistic performance estimate.

resources.text: Implement K-Fold from scratch to understand the mechanics

26.desc: Regularization adds a penalty to the loss function to discourage overly complex models. Ridge (L2), Lasso (L1), and ElasticNet are the three main variants.
concepts: L1 Regularization (Lasso) — sparse weights, feature selection
ElasticNet — hybrid of L1 and L2
Dropout in neural networks — same intuition
26.why: Overfitting is universal in ML. Regularization is the primary defence. Lasso can simultaneously fit a model and select features.

resources.text: Plot coefficient paths as alpha increases — understand sparsity

27.desc: A neural network is composed of layers of artificial neurons (perceptrons). The MLP is the foundational architecture — understanding it unlocks all of deep learning.
concepts: MLP — input layer, hidden layers, output layer
27.why: Every advanced architecture (CNN, RNN, Transformer) is built from the same building blocks as the MLP. The perceptron is the foundation of the entire deep learning stack.

resources.text: Implement a 2-layer MLP from scratch in NumPy (XOR)
Neural Networks and Deep Learning by Michael Nielsen (free)

28.desc: Forward propagation computes predictions. Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss w.r.t. every weight using the chain rule — enabling gradient descent to train the network.
concepts: Chain Rule applied to nested functions
Gradient of MSE and Cross-Entropy w.r.t. weights
28.why: Backpropagation is the single algorithm that makes deep learning work. Without understanding it you cannot debug training failures or exploding gradients.

resources.text: Implement backprop from scratch in NumPy — do not skip this

29.desc: Activation functions introduce non-linearity so networks can learn complex patterns. Loss functions measure the error between predictions and ground truth.
concepts: Sigmoid, Tanh — saturation and vanishing gradient
Leaky ReLU, ELU, GELU — solving dying ReLU
29.why: Choosing the wrong activation in deep networks causes vanishing gradients. The right loss function defines what your model actually optimizes for.

resources.text: Plot activation functions and their gradients

30.desc: PyTorch, TensorFlow, and Keras provide automatic differentiation, GPU support, and pre-built layers — eliminating the need to implement backprop manually.
concepts: nn.Module — defining custom layers and models
Training loop: forward -> loss -> backward -> step
30.why: PyTorch is the dominant framework for research and production. Knowing it deeply means you can implement any architecture from a paper.

resources.text: Build MNIST classifier with PyTorch from scratch

31.desc: CNNs use convolutional filters to detect spatial hierarchies in images — edges, textures, objects. They are the backbone of computer vision.
31.why: Every production vision system (face recognition, medical imaging, autonomous driving) is built on CNNs. This is the entry point to computer vision.

resources.text: Build CNN for CIFAR-10 in PyTorch from scratch
ResNet paper — Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

32.desc: CNNs power tasks beyond classification — semantic segmentation (pixel labels), object detection (bounding boxes), and video understanding.
concepts: Object Detection — YOLO, Faster R-CNN, SSD
32.why: Knowing CNN applications separates someone who trained MNIST from someone who can build real vision products.

resources.text: YOLO paper series — fast object detection
torchvision — pretrained models and detection datasets
U-Net paper — semantic segmentation for medical imaging

33.desc: RNNs process sequential data by maintaining a hidden state. LSTMs and GRUs solve the vanishing gradient problem enabling learning of long-range dependencies.
concepts: Bidirectional RNN — reads sequence both ways
33.why: Understanding RNNs is required to understand attention mechanisms and Transformers — their natural evolution.

resources.text: Build char-level language model with LSTM in PyTorch

34.desc: Attention mechanisms allow models to focus on relevant parts of an input — solving the bottleneck of encoding entire sequences into a single fixed vector.
concepts: Scaled Dot-Product Attention — Q, K, V matrices
Self-Attention — attending to the same sequence
34.why: Attention is the direct predecessor of Transformers. Understanding the Q/K/V mechanism is required to understand BERT, GPT, and every modern LLM.

resources.text: Attention Is All You Need paper (Vaswani et al., 2017)
Implement scaled dot-product attention from scratch in PyTorch

35.desc: Autoencoders learn a compressed latent representation of data through an encoder-decoder structure trained to reconstruct its input.
concepts: Encoder — compresses input to latent code z
35.why: Autoencoders underpin dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection, image generation (VAE), and are the conceptual precursor to diffusion models.

resources.text: Lilian Weng blog — From Autoencoder to Beta-VAE
Build denoising autoencoder on MNIST in PyTorch
VAE paper — Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes (Kingma & Welling)

36.desc: GANs train two networks in adversarial competition — a generator produces fake data, a discriminator tries to distinguish fake from real. The result: photorealistic generative models.
36.why: GANs produced the first photorealistic synthetic images and remain relevant for data augmentation, style transfer, and image-to-image translation.

resources.text: Original GAN paper — Goodfellow et al. 2014
Build DCGAN for MNIST digit generation in PyTorch
Lilian Weng — From GAN to WGAN (comprehensive blog)

37.desc: Transformers replaced RNNs as the dominant sequence model. Using only self-attention (no recurrence), they process sequences in parallel — enabling the LLM revolution.
concepts: Self-Attention — all tokens attend to all tokens
37.why: BERT, GPT, LLaMA, Stable Diffusion — every frontier AI model is a Transformer. This is the single most important architecture in modern AI.

resources.text: Attention Is All You Need paper — read it closely
Implement Transformer encoder from scratch in PyTorch
Jay Alammar — The Illustrated Transformer (essential blog)

38.desc: NLP preprocessing converts raw text into numerical representations. Tokenization, stemming, lemmatization, and word embeddings are the core pipeline steps.
38.why: All NLP starts here. Even with LLMs, understanding tokenization (BPE, SentencePiece) is critical — it affects context length, cost, and multilingual performance.

resources.text: Natural Language Processing with Python (NLTK book, free)
Gensim Word2Vec — train on custom corpus, visualize with t-SNE

39.desc: BERT and GPT are the two dominant pretraining paradigms that power modern NLP — from sentiment analysis to question answering to text generation.
concepts: Sentence classification, NER, QA with BERT
39.why: BERT/GPT-style models are the industry standard for all NLP tasks. If you work with text in production, you will fine-tune or prompt these models daily.

resources.text: HuggingFace — fine-tune BERT for sentiment on IMDB

40.desc: Reinforcement Learning trains agents to take actions to maximize cumulative reward. Q-Learning and DQN use neural networks to approximate optimal action-value functions.
40.why: RL powers game-playing AI (AlphaGo), robotics control, and RLHF — the training technique behind ChatGPT.

resources.text: Sutton & Barto — RL: An Introduction (free PDF)
DQN paper — Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning

41.desc: Policy Gradient methods directly optimize the policy using gradient ascent on expected reward. Actor-Critic combines value-based and policy-based methods.
concepts: Policy function pi(a|s) — parametric action selection
REINFORCE algorithm — Monte Carlo policy gradient
Actor-Critic — separate value and policy networks
41.why: PPO is the algorithm behind ChatGPT's RLHF training and most production robotics. Policy gradient methods handle continuous action spaces that DQN cannot.

resources.text: Spinning Up in Deep RL — OpenAI (free, comprehensive)
PPO paper — Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms

42.desc: Recommendation Systems predict what users will like based on past behaviour and similarities. Collaborative filtering, matrix factorization, and embedding models are the core techniques.
42.why: Recommenders drive revenue at Netflix, YouTube, Amazon, and Spotify. Matrix factorization and embedding models are transferable to any domain.

resources.text: Koren et al. — Matrix Factorization Techniques
Surprise library — collaborative filtering in Python

43.desc: Explainable AI (XAI) provides tools to understand why a model makes specific predictions — critical for trust, debugging, fairness audits, and regulatory compliance.
43.why: In healthcare, finance, and law, black-box models are legally prohibited or ethically unacceptable. XAI is now a production requirement.

resources.text: shap.TreeExplainer — SHAP for XGBoost and Random Forest
Interpretable ML book — Christoph Molnar (free PDF)

44.desc: Self-supervised learning generates supervision from unlabelled data itself. Semi-supervised learning uses both labelled and unlabelled data to improve performance.
concepts: Pseudo-Labelling — confident unlabelled predictions as labels
Label efficiency — how much labelled data is needed?
44.why: Labelling data is expensive. Self-supervised pretraining (BERT, GPT, Vision MAE) achieves strong results with minimal labels. This is how frontier models are trained.

resources.text: SimCLR paper — A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning

45.desc: Model selection picks the best algorithm. Hyperparameter tuning finds the optimal configuration. Together they bridge trained model and production-ready model.
concepts: Randomized Search — random sampling of parameter space
Early Stopping — prevent overfitting during tuning
Warm Starting — continue tuning from previous run
45.why: Default hyperparameters are almost never optimal. Proper tuning routinely improves performance by 5-15%. Bayesian optimization is now the industry standard.

46.desc: Production ML requires robust data pipelines — splitting data correctly, loading batches efficiently, preventing leakage, and handling distributional shift over time.
46.why: More production ML failures are caused by incorrect data pipelines than bad models. A leaky pipeline makes your model look perfect in testing and fail in production.

resources.text: sklearn Pipeline docs — compose preprocessing + model
PyTorch Dataset & DataLoader — custom dataset class

47.desc: Model serving deploys trained models to production. FastAPI + Docker is the standard lightweight stack for ML APIs.
concepts: Model serialization — joblib, pickle, ONNX, TorchScript
FastAPI — async REST API for ML
47.why: A model that is not deployed is worthless. Knowing how to serve models with FastAPI and Docker turns research into product.

resources.text: Build a /predict POST endpoint for an sklearn model

48.desc: Advanced scikit-learn covers building reusable, production-grade pipelines with custom transformers, column transformers, and feature unions.
concepts: ColumnTransformer — different transforms per feature type
FunctionTransformer — wrap any function as transformer
48.why: Clean, reusable sklearn Pipelines prevent data leakage, make deployment trivial, and ensure train/inference consistency. This is how professional ML engineers write production code.

resources.text: Build a custom TextCleaner transformer class from scratch
Hands-On ML by Geron — Pipelines chapter

01.desc: Linear Algebra is the mathematics of vectors, matrices, and linear transformations — the most critical math prerequisite for ML.
01.why: Neural networks are chains of matrix multiplications. PCA, SVD, and attention are all linear algebra. Without this you cannot understand what your models compute.

resources.text: Gilbert Strang — Introduction to Linear Algebra (MIT)
numpy.linalg docs — practice every operation in code

02.desc: Calculus gives us the tools to optimize ML models. Derivatives measure how a function changes and gradient descent uses this to minimize loss functions.
02.why: Backpropagation is the chain rule applied to a computation graph. Every optimizer relies on gradients. You cannot debug training without understanding calculus.

resources.text: PyTorch autograd — see calculus in action

03.desc: Descriptive statistics summarizes the main features of a dataset. It is your first lens for understanding data before any model is trained.
03.why: Every ML project starts with EDA. If you cannot describe your data, you will make wrong modelling decisions — garbage in, garbage out.

resources.text: Think Stats by Allen Downey (free PDF)
Kaggle — practice EDA on Titanic, Iris

04.desc: Inferential statistics lets you draw conclusions about a population from a sample. Bayes Theorem is the framework for updating beliefs given new evidence.
04.why: A/B testing, confidence intervals, and Bayesian models all require this. It prevents you from fooling yourself with statistically insignificant results.

05.desc: Python is the dominant language for ML. You need solid fundamentals — clean OOP, data structures, and the ability to write reusable modular code.
05.why: Every ML library is Python. You will write custom layers, data loaders, and pipelines — you need fluent Python, not just hello-world.

resources.text: LeetCode Easy problems — reinforce logic & data structures

06.desc: NumPy provides fast N-dimensional arrays and mathematical operations that form the backbone of every ML library.
06.why: Pandas, scikit-learn, and PyTorch all use NumPy arrays internally. If you cannot vectorize your code your models will be 100x slower.

resources.text: From Python to NumPy by Nicolas Rougier (free PDF)

07.desc: Pandas is the go-to library for data manipulation and analysis. Think Excel in Python — but far more powerful, programmable, and reproducible.
07.why: Real-world data is always messy. You will spend 60-80% of any ML project wrangling data in Pandas.

resources.text: Pandas official docs — 10 minutes to pandas
Python for Data Analysis by Wes McKinney

08.desc: Matplotlib and Seaborn are the core plotting libraries. Visualization is how you understand data, communicate insights, and debug model behaviour.
08.why: A model that cannot be visualized cannot be fully understood or trusted. Charts catch data leakage and class imbalance that tables miss.

resources.text: Kaggle — EDA notebooks on any dataset

09.desc: ML systems need data from databases, APIs, and IoT streams. Knowing how to acquire structured and unstructured data is the first step in any real pipeline.
concepts: SQL — SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, subqueries
09.why: You will rarely be handed a clean CSV. Production ML systems pull from databases, APIs, and streaming sources.
